title: Felting crochet fabric
subtitle: Wet felting a crochet piece in the washing machine to produce dense, stiff felt
excerpt: Felting crochet fabric uses heat, agitation, and moisture to mat the fibres of a wool piece together into a dense, stiff fabric with no visible stitch structure. The piece shrinks considerably in the process. You crochet larger than the finished size you want, then felt down to it.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework, 1886, Project Gutenberg #20776. Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing). Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: A process in which wool fibres are matted together through heat, agitation, and moisture, causing the scales on the fibre shaft to interlock permanently. The resulting fabric is dense, stiff, and does not unravel at cut edges.

Strictly, fulling applies to woven or knitted fabric that has already been constructed; felting applies to loose fibres. In common use, both terms describe the process of shrinking and matting wool fabric through washing.

content.text: crochet fabric means deliberately subjecting a wool piece to the conditions that would ruin a finished garment: heat, agitation, and water. The result is a dense, stiff felt fabric with no visible stitch structure. The piece shrinks by a third to a half of its original dimensions. This is intentional; you crochet the piece at a large, loose gauge and felt it down to the finished size.

Only 100% wool or other animal fibres felt reliably. Superwash-treated wool and synthetic fibres will not felt; the process only works on untreated protein fibres. Check the yarn label before starting. If the label says machine washable or superwash, the yarn will not felt.

items.name: 100% wool yarn, not superwash-treated
items.note: Aran or chunky weight felts quickly. Fine-weight wool can take many cycles to felt and may not shrink as dramatically.

items.name: Crochet hook 2 sizes larger than the label recommends
items.note: A loose, open crochet gauge felts better than a tight one. The open fabric gives the fibres room to move and mat together.

items.name: Washing machine
items.note: Hot cycle with agitation. Top-loaders with an agitator typically felt faster than front-loaders.

items.name: Mesh laundry bag
items.note: Prevents fibres from clogging the washing machine filter

items.name: Tennis balls or rubber dryer balls
items.note: Added to the machine to increase agitation

items.name: Blocking mat and pins
items.note: For shaping the piece to the correct dimensions while still warm and damp

content.text: Crochet the piece at the pre-felt dimensions. Weave in all ends securely. If the piece has handles or straps, sew any joins firmly; felt locks everything together, but a weak seam before felting can still fail.
Place the piece in a mesh laundry bag with the tennis balls. The bag catches shed fibres; the balls add agitation.
Run the washing machine on a hot cycle with a small amount of liquid detergent (not powder). Do not use a delicates or wool cycle, as these are designed to prevent felting.
Check the piece after 10 minutes. The stitch structure should be starting to blur. If individual stitches are still clearly visible, run for a further 10 minutes and check again.
When the piece has reached the target dimensions, remove it from the machine immediately. Do not leave it in a hot machine; felting continues while the piece remains hot and wet.

Shape the piece while warm: pin it to the blocking mat at the correct dimensions, insert formers into bags and bowls (a plastic container the right size works well), and stuff hats with newspaper. Leave to dry completely.
is sometimes used for this process. In strict usage, fulling applies to fabric that has already been constructed; both terms describe the same result in practice.

items.symptom: The piece is not felting after two full washing cycles
items.cause: The yarn is either superwash-treated or contains synthetic fibre.
items.fix: Test a yarn swatch in boiling water with agitation before starting the main project. If the swatch does not felt, the yarn will not felt in the machine either.

items.symptom: The piece shrank more than intended
items.cause: The felting cycle ran too long, or the starting gauge was tighter than needed.
items.fix: For future projects, check the piece every 5 minutes once shrinkage begins. Remove it as soon as target dimensions are reached. Felting cannot be reversed.

items.symptom: The finished piece is stiff but patchy, with some areas more felted than others
items.cause: Uneven agitation in the machine, or the piece was bunched in one position for the whole cycle.
items.fix: In future, remove the piece from the machine halfway through and re-position it in the bag. In front-loaders, agitation is less vigorous in spots; a second cycle often evens the result.

content.text: A simple round bowl is the standard first felting project. Work a flat circle about 35 cm in diameter in aran-weight 100% wool at a 7 mm hook. After felting it should be about 20 to 22 cm across and stiff enough to hold its shape as a bowl. Push the centre down while the felt is still warm to create the bowl form, and leave it to dry supported on a dish of the right size.
